newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: World peace calls grow, Kabul ex-rulers seize base.
newsitem.headline: World peace calls grow, Kabul ex-rulers seize base.

text.p: World calls for peace in Afghanistan widened as the ousted government said its forces, backed by new military allies, seized a major airbase near Taleban-occupied Kabul.

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said in Hamburg, Germany, the United Nations would keep on trying to broker peace, but had no immediate plans to send an interim peacekeeping force to the capital.
He said the U.N. would continue to seek ways to demilitarise the city, which the Taleban Islamic militia took three weeks ago. But he stressed all warring parties would have to agree.

A Taleban evacuation of Kabul was floated at the United Nations. The United States called it "probably premature", although State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said a proposal to demilitarise Kabul was "an important idea".
Forces of the ousted administration said they staged a joint attack with new-found ethnic Uzbek allies and drove Taleban Islamic fighters from the important Bagram military base.

The assault was mounted by troops of the former government's military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, backed for the first time by fighters from Uzbek military commander Abdul Rashid Dostum from northern Afghanistan, using tanks, artillery and mortars.

Dostum sent a dozen tanks and several hundred men to join Masood on Thursday after formally recognising the government driven from Kabul and promising to back Masood if the Taleban did not stop fighting.

"Now we have control of all of the airport at Bagram, the main part of the Taleban force has retreated along the new road back towards Kabul," said an official, Mirabbuddin Astana, at Masood's headquarters.
Masood's men previously controlled about half the airbase, 60 km (40 miles) north of Kabul, with Taleban holding the other half.
Masood earlier told Taleban fighters to quit the Afghan capital.
Iran expressed concern over the crisis boiling over to neighbouring Central Asian states, Tehran radio reported.
"It is natural for us to be concerned that, God forbid, this (Afghan) turmoil would spread to Central Asia," Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati told state-run radio.
Central Asian states shared Iran's concern, said Velayati, on return from a lightning tour of the region and India.
Shi'ite Moslem Iran recognises the government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani, ousted from Kabul by the radical Sunni Taleban militia.
Iranian media have accused Pakistan of setting up the Taleban with backing from the United States and funding from Saudi Arabia to counter Iran's influence in the region.
Pakistan denies the charges.
Pakistani President Farooq Leghari left for Uzbekistan with the Afghan conflict likely to dominate talks with President Islam Karimov.
Leghari, due to visit Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan later this month, is expected to reassure his Central Asian hosts that Taleban has no territorial ambitions beyond Afghanistan's borders.
Masood, a former defence minister, urged the Taleban to cede Kabul to a U.N. force and blamed other factions for letting the turbanned Islamist warriors capture the city in the first place.
The head of one of the world's leading Islamic institutions called on Afghans to halt their fratricidal war and live together in peace.

"We ask you, we appeal to you, brothers and sons to lay down your weapons and to live all together as loving brothers," Mohammed Sayed Tantawi, Grand Sheikh of Cairo's al-Azhar University, said during a visit to Islamabad.
